content.content:
1	# ChronicleFlow
2	
3	ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
4	workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
5	SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.
6	
7	The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:
8	
9	- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, bounded
10	  `loop`, and dynamic `map` nodes;
11	- a workflow may declare named versions: every declared version is kept and
12	  each execution is bound to the version that was current (or explicitly
13	  named) when it started, so upgrading a workflow never changes a running
14	  execution, and a running execution can be explicitly migrated to another
15	  version of the same workflow, after which it advances under that version;
16	- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
17	  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
18	- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
19	  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
20	  execution;
21	- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
22	  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
23	  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
24	  execution with reason `rejected`);
25	- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
26	  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
27	- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
28	  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
29	- a map node inside a loop body expands independently in every iteration
30	  from that iteration's source output, its instances and events belonging
31	  to the iteration they expanded in;
32	- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
33	- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
34	- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
35	  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
36	  latest checkpoint after a restart;
37	- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
38	  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
39	  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
40	  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
41	- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
42	- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
43	  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
44	  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
45	- subscriptions may also declare queue targets instead of webhook addresses:
46	  matching business events are appended, in occurrence order, to persistent
47	  per-execution queues that callers pull from and acknowledge explicitly,
48	  with a visibility timeout returning unacknowledged messages to the pending
49	  set (delivery is at least once);
50	- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
51	  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
52	  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
53	  resumed, periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
54	  skipped, according to the declared missed policy, and a read-only preview
55	  query projects the upcoming trigger times and their inputs.
56	
57	## Requirements
58	
59	- Python 3.11 or newer
60	- no third-party runtime dependencies
61	
62	## Run the service
63	
64	```bash
65	PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
66	```
67	
68	The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
69	has bound the port.
70	
71	## HTTP API
72	
73	All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.
74	
75	Responses are compact JSON with no insignificant whitespace, and every
76	response body ends with exactly one trailing newline (`\n`). Numbers
77	round-trip with their full precision: finite floats keep their original
78	IEEE-754 value through the shortest textual representation that decodes to
79	it (so `0.30000000000000004` stays `0.30000000000000004`), negative zero is
80	preserved as `-0.0`, and integers stay integers. Non-finite numbers may
81	never appear in a request and are never produced in a response; timestamps
82	are ISO-8601 UTC strings ending in `Z`.
83	
84	### Tenants and quotas
85	
86	A request may declare a tenant by sending the `X-Tenant-Id` header with a
87	non-empty identifier. Every workflow, execution, schedule, schedule status,
88	delivery history, and queue record is scoped to the tenant of the request that
89	created it: queries and operations only ever see data belonging to that
90	tenant, and different tenants may use the same workflow or execution
91	identifiers without colliding. Referencing another tenant's resource — for
92	example advancing, migrating, deciding, claiming, cancelling, recovering, replaying, or
93	reading the events, checkpoints, deliveries, queues, or schedule of an execution or
94	workflow owned by another tenant, or pulling from or acknowledging one of its
95	queues — is answered exactly like a reference to a
96	missing resource: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the resource
97	exists elsewhere. An execution created in one tenant can only reference a
98	workflow of the same tenant, and a migration can only name a version of that
99	workflow in the same tenant; referencing an unseen workflow identifier or
100	version is the usual `404 not_found`.
101	
102	The header applies to every workflow, execution, and schedule entry point,
103	including creation, advancement, migration, approval decisions, lease
104	operations, cancellation, recovery, replay, instance deletion and
105	modification and re-expansion, queue pulls, acknowledgements, and all
106	history and status queries, as well as the quota and price declarations,
107	the price read, and the usage, bill, and metrics queries. An empty
108	`X-Tenant-Id` value is a `400 validation_error`. Requests that omit the
109	header entirely keep using the single legacy namespace, whose advancement,
110	approvals, leases, retries, timeouts, cancellation, checkpoints, recovery,
111	scheduling, and replay behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged: the tenant is
112	stored only as database scope, never added to a state field or event payload,
113	and state shapes and event streams gain no new fields. Idempotency keys are
114	scoped per tenant as well, so tenants can never see or collide with each
115	other's keys; reusing a key for another operation within the same tenant is
116	the usual `409 conflict`.
117	
118	A tenant may declare quotas bounding how many workflows and executions it may
119	hold:
120	
121	```http
122	PUT /quotas
123	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-1
124	X-Tenant-Id: acme
125	
126	{"workflows": 10, "executions": 100}
127	```
128	
129	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must contain exactly
130	`workflows` and `executions`, each a positive integer; a non-positive,
131	non-integer, boolean, or non-finite value, a missing or extra field, or a
132	non-object body is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Both quota
133	routes require a tenant: calling them without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
134	one) is a `400 validation_error`. The response is
135	`{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100}}`; declaring again replaces the
136	limits (re-anchoring nothing else). Lowering a limit below the current
137	holding deletes no existing data — existing workflows and executions stay
138	fully usable — it only rejects later writes that would exceed the new limit.
139	
140	```http
141	GET /quotas
142	X-Tenant-Id: acme
143	```
144	
145	Returns the declared quota, or the definite empty result `{"quota":null}`
146	when the tenant has declared none.
147	
148	When a write would take the tenant past either limit, the whole request is
149	rejected with `409 conflict` and an error message that names the quota (for
150	example `quota exceeded: tenant already holds 10 workflows (quota limit is
151	10)`), so callers can tell quota rejection apart from an ordinary identifier
152	conflict. The rejection performs no partial write: nothing is inserted and
153	previously stored data is unaffected, exactly as for validation failures.
154	
155	A schedule firing on time creates its execution in the schedule's tenant and
156	that execution counts against the tenant's execution quota. When the tenant
157	is at its execution limit, the due period creates no execution and the
158	schedule is left unchanged — its cursor, `last_triggered_at`, and
159	`last_execution_id` stay as they were — so the period is settled on a later
160	pass once capacity exists, under the usual per-period idempotence. Delivery
161	history follows the tenant of the execution it belongs to.
162	
163	### Tenant price tables
164	
165	The bill's baseline unit prices are built in. A tenant may instead declare
166	its own price table on a separate entry point with the same calling shape as
167	the quota declaration:
168	
169	```http
170	PUT /prices
171	Idempotency-Key: price-request-1
172	X-Tenant-Id: acme
173	
174	{"execution_started":200,"workflow_created":1500}
175	```
176	
177	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must be a non-empty
178	JSON object giving a map of metered action type to a positive-integer unit
179	price in cents. A non-positive, non-integer, boolean, or non-finite price,
180	an unknown metered type, a missing field (an empty object), an extra field
181	that is not a metered type, or a non-object body is a `400
182	validation_error` that writes nothing. Both price routes require a tenant:
183	calling them without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty one) is a `400
184	validation_error`, and an unknown query parameter on the read is rejected
185	the same way. The response is
186	`{"prices":{"execution_started":200,"workflow_created":1500}}`, with the
187	declared types in ascending type-identifier order.
188	
189	A successful declaration replaces the tenant's price table as a whole with
190	exactly the types given this time; metered types the declaration does not
191	name fall back to the built-in default prices when a bill is taken. The
192	declaration rewrites no recorded usage counts and changes no bill taken
193	before it was made.
194	
195	```http
196	GET /prices
197	X-Tenant-Id: acme
198	```
199	
200	Returns the price table currently declared by the tenant, in ascending
201	type-identifier order, or the definite empty result `{"prices":null}` for a
202	tenant that has never declared one. The stored table lists only the types
203	the declaration named; types left at the default are not copied into it.
204	
205	The declaration follows the same idempotency rules as every other write:
206	the `Idempotency-Key` header is required, repeating the same declaration
207	with the same key returns the first result and performs no second
208	replacement, and reusing a key for another operation — including another
209	price declaration — in the same tenant is a `409 conflict` that leaves the
210	tenant's price table unchanged. Price tables are scoped per tenant like
211	everything else: a tenant can never read another's declaration, and another
212	tenant's declaration never affects this tenant's bill amounts.
213	
214	The bill and the bucketed bill price with the price table in effect **at
215	query time**: a named type uses the tenant's declared price and every other
216	type uses the built-in default. Each returned line still gives the metered
217	type, the actual `unit_price` used, the `count`, and the integer-cent
218	`subtotal`, and the total is exactly the sum of the listed subtotals; types
219	with no matching record are still omitted rather than listed at zero. A
220	declaration affects only later queries — it neither rewrites recorded usage
221	nor revises historical bills — changes no metering, and leaves the bill and
222	usage queries read-only. There is no delete entry point in this release; a
223	declared table can only be replaced by another declaration.
224	
225	### Usage metering and billing
226	
227	Requests that carry a tenant identifier leave a usage record for each billable
228	action they perform. Only tenant-scoped requests are metered: a request that
229	omits the `X-Tenant-Id` header keeps the legacy namespace and writes no usage
230	record at all, with its state shapes and event content unchanged. The four
231	metered action types are:
232	
233	- `workflow_created` — a workflow definition is stored. Adding a new version
234	  to an existing workflow is one workflow creation, the same as the first
235	  definition;
236	- `execution_started` — an execution is created and starts `running`;
237	- `schedule_triggered` — a due schedule period creates its execution. The
238	  scheduled execution is metered both as `execution_started` and as
239	  `schedule_triggered`;
240	- `delivery_attempted` — one outbound webhook HTTP attempt is made, or one
241	  queue message is delivered to a caller pulling from a queue. A
242	  subscription that retries is metered once per attempt, so a delivery that
243	  fails and then succeeds on its second attempt records two attempts; the
244	  action is metered whether it ultimately succeeds or fails. A queue pull
245	  meters one attempt per message it delivers, so a redelivery after the
246	  visibility timeout is metered again, while a pull that delivers nothing
247	  meters nothing.
248	
249	Metering is atomic with the action it describes: a write rejected by
250	validation or by a quota produces no record and performs no partial write.
251	Repeating an idempotent command returns its first result and writes no second
252	record, and settling the same schedule period more than once (a repeated
253	trigger or a later pass) meters that period only once. Replay, recovery, and
254	queries never meter and never alter recorded usage or billing conclusions.
255	
256	```http
257	GET /usage
258	X-Tenant-Id: acme
259	```
260	
261	Returns `{"usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}`: the
262	cumulative count of recorded actions per type, sorted by ascending type
263	identifier. Types with no records are omitted, so a tenant with no usage gets
264	the definite empty result `{"usage":[]}`.
265	
266	```http
267	GET /bill
268	X-Tenant-Id: acme
269	```
270	
271	Returns the per-type bill:
272	
273	```json
274	{"bill":{"items":[
275	  {"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100},
276	  {"type":"workflow_created","count":2,"unit_price":1000,"subtotal":2000}
277	],"total":2100}}
278	```
279	
280	Each item gives the metered `count`, a positive-integer `unit_price` in cents
281	that is also returned in the response, and a `subtotal` equal to
282	`count * unit_price`; `total` is the integer-cent sum of every subtotal. With
283	no records, `items` is empty and `total` is `0`. The price used per type is
284	the tenant's declared price when its price table names that type and the
285	built-in default otherwise, read from the table in effect at query time (see
286	[Tenant price tables](#tenant-price-tables)); tenants with no declaration are
287	billed byte for byte as before.
288	
289	Both endpoints accept the same optional query parameters the events and
290	metrics queries accept: an optional metered-type filter and an ISO-8601 UTC
291	timestamp window, each timestamp ending in `Z`, plus an optional fixed time
292	bucket:
293	
294	```http
295	GET /usage?type=execution_started,workflow_created&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
296	GET /bill?type=execution_started&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
297	X-Tenant-Id: acme
298	```
299	
300	- `type` names one metered action type or a comma-separated set of them; only
301	  records whose type is in the set are counted. A single identifier needs no
302	  comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown metered type is a
303	  `400 validation_error`; when `type` is absent every type is counted, exactly
304	  as before;
305	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on each usage record's
306	  occurrence time: a record whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted.
307	  When either parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting
308	  both returns exactly the cumulative result above;
309	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
310	  parameter is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing;
311	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
312	  simply contains no records. Usage then reports the definite empty result
313	  `{"usage":[]}`, and the bill reports an empty `items` list with a `total` of
314	  `0`.
315	
316	The type filter and the time window apply together as an intersection: a
317	record is counted only when its type is named **and** its occurrence time is
318	in the window. A type the filter names but that has no matching record is
319	omitted rather than reported at zero, so a filter that matches nothing gives
320	the same definite empty results as an empty window: `{"usage":[]}` for usage
321	and an empty `items` list with a `total` of `0` for the bill.
322	
323	Both endpoints also accept an optional `bucket` parameter for a fixed-bucket
324	trend summary, so callers never have to pull records and group them
325	themselves:
326	
327	```http
328	GET /usage?bucket=hour&since=2026-09-26T00:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-27T00:00:00.000Z
329	GET /bill?bucket=day&type=execution_started
330	X-Tenant-Id: acme
331	```
332	
333	- `bucket` is exactly `hour` or `day`: `hour` buckets start on the UTC hour
334	  and `day` buckets at UTC midnight, both aligned solely to UTC. An empty or
335	  any other value is a `400 validation_error`, exactly like a repeated
336	  parameter or an unknown query parameter;
337	- when `bucket` is present, usage returns
338	  `{"usage_buckets":[{"bucket_start":"2026-09-26T08:00:00Z","usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}, ...]}`:
339	  the buckets with at least one matching record, in ascending bucket-start
340	  order. Each entry gives its `bucket_start` first — an ISO-8601 UTC string
341	  ending in `Z` at the hour or midnight — followed by `usage`, the per-type
342	  counts inside that bucket in ascending type-identifier order; a type with no
343	  record in the bucket is omitted;
344	- when `bucket` is present, the bill returns
345	  `{"bill":{"buckets":[{"bucket_start":"2026-09-26T00:00:00Z","items":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100}, ...],"subtotal":100}, ...],"total":100}}`.
346	  Buckets appear in ascending bucket-start order; each bucket's `items` stay
347	  sorted by ascending type identifier, each line giving the filtered count,
348	  the usual positive-integer `unit_price`, and an integer-cent `subtotal` of
349	  the two, and a type with no matching record is omitted rather than reported
350	  at zero. Each bucket also carries its own `subtotal`, and the window
351	  `total` is exactly the sum of the listed per-bucket subtotals, all amounts
352	  integer cents;
353	- a bucket that holds no matching record never appears, so an empty tenant, a
354	  window with `since` later than `until`, or a filter that matches nothing
355	  returns the definite empty bucket lists `{"usage_buckets":[]}` and
356	  `{"bill":{"buckets":[],"total":0}` — never an error, with the empty bill's
357	  total at `0`;
358	- bucketing applies together with the type filter and the time window as an
359	  intersection: a bucket holds only records whose occurrence time is in the
360	  closed window **and** whose type the filter names. The window keeps its
361	  closed endpoints, its open bounds when either side is omitted, and the
362	  existing rule for when a record's instant falls in it; buckets are simply
363	  the same matching records rolled up to their UTC bucket;
364	- the bucketed queries are read-only like the others: they append no usage
365	  records, change no metering basis or prices, and never alter recorded usage
366	  or billing conclusions — under event replay or recovery the same window,
367	  type filter, and bucket always give the same answer;
368	- omitting `bucket` leaves both queries exactly as before: the same compact
369	  JSON responses with `usage` / `items` shapes, full float precision and the
370	  `-0.0` convention, byte for byte. The parameter introduces no second
371	  protocol and changes no entry point's existing behavior.
372	
373	Only records whose occurrence time falls in the window are counted. Within
374	the window the bill keeps the same basis as always: each present type reports
375	its filtered, windowed count, its usual `unit_price`, and a `subtotal` of the
376	two; items stay sorted by ascending type identifier, and a type with no
377	matching record is omitted rather than reported at zero. The bill's `total`
378	is exactly the sum of the subtotals of the listed items. The query is
379	read-only: it writes no usage records, changes no prices or metering
380	conclusions, and never alters already recorded usage — under event replay or
381	recovery the same window and type filter always give the same answer.
382	
383	Both endpoints are tenant-scoped `GET` requests: a missing or empty
384	`X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error` that reveals no usage. Usage and
385	bill data follow the usual tenant isolation, so one tenant can never see
386	another's records under any type filter or window, and another tenant's
387	records never affect this tenant's counts or totals.
388	
389	### Per-record usage history
390	
391	The cumulative usage query reports only per-type totals. A separate endpoint
392	returns the individual usage records themselves, so each billed action can be
393	checked against the moment it occurred:
394	
395	```http
396	GET /usage/records?limit=50
397	X-Tenant-Id: acme
398	```
399	
400	Returns `{"records":[...]}` with the matching records in ascending order of
401	occurrence time; records sharing one instant are ordered by ascending
402	sequence. Each record is:
403	
404	```json
405	{"sequence":7,"type":"execution_started","occurred_at":"2026-09-26T08:30:00.000Z"}
406	```
407	
408	- `sequence` is a stable, strictly increasing positive integer per tenant. It
409	  identifies the record across every query and is never renumbered by a
410	  filter or a page;
411	- `type` is the metered action type;
412	- `occurred_at` is the record's occurrence time as an ISO-8601 UTC string
413	  ending in `Z`.
414	
415	A tenant with no matching records gets the definite empty result
416	`{"records":[]}`, never an error. The response ends with a single newline,
417	like every other JSON endpoint.
418	
419	The endpoint accepts an optional metered-type filter, the same optional
420	closed time window the events and usage queries accept, plus cursor
421	pagination:
422	
423	```http
424	GET /usage/records?type=execution_started,workflow_created&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
425	```
426	
427	- `type` names one metered action type or a comma-separated set of them;
428	  only records whose type is in the set are returned. A single identifier
429	  needs no comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown metered
430	  type is a `400 validation_error`; when `type` is absent every type is
431	  returned, exactly as before;
432	- `since` and `until` are ISO-8601 UTC timestamps ending in `Z` and bind a
433	  **closed** interval on each record's occurrence time: a record whose time
434	  equals either boundary is included. When either is absent the corresponding
435	  bound is open; when `since` is later than `until` the window matches
436	  nothing and the definite empty list is returned;
437	- `limit` is **required** and must be a positive integer; a page never
438	  contains more than that many records;
439	- `cursor` is the `sequence` of the previous page's last record; only records
440	  whose `sequence` is strictly greater are returned, so pages neither overlap
441	  nor skip. It is omitted on the first page and must be a positive integer;
442	- the type filter, time window, and pagination apply together as an
443	  intersection, and filtering never changes a record's `sequence`.
444	
445	A malformed timestamp, an unknown, empty, or duplicated `type` entry, a
446	missing or non-positive-integer `limit`, a non-positive-integer `cursor`, a
447	repeated parameter, or any unknown query parameter is a `400
448	validation_error` that writes nothing. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a
449	`400 validation_error` that reveals no records. The query is read-only: it
450	appends no usage records, writes no events, and changes no metering, prices,
451	quotas, or billing conclusions. Records follow the usual tenant isolation, so
452	another tenant's records are never visible under any type filter, window, or
453	page and never affect this tenant's result; replay and recovery leave every
454	recorded sequence, time, and billing conclusion unchanged.
455	
456	### Operational metrics
457	
458	```http
459	GET /metrics
460	X-Tenant-Id: acme
461	```
462	
463	Returns one line of compact JSON summarizing the business facts already
464	recorded for the tenant, ending with the usual single newline. The endpoint
465	is read-only: it appends no events, writes no usage records, and changes no
466	stored data, and it reports only persisted facts — it performs no
467	advancement, approval, recovery, or replay of its own, so those operations
468	never change what a metrics query observes beyond the facts they themselves
469	recorded. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`, and
470	the metrics follow the usual tenant isolation: another tenant's facts are
471	never visible in any dimension and never affect this tenant's counts. A
472	tenant with no recorded facts at all gets the definite empty result with
473	every dimension at zero — not an error. With no query parameters the answer
474	is every fact recorded for the tenant, byte for byte.
475	
476	The query accepts two optional query parameters, each an ISO-8601 UTC
477	timestamp ending in `Z`:
478	
479	```http
480	GET /metrics?since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
481	X-Tenant-Id: acme
482	```
483	
484	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on the facts' occurrence
485	  times: a fact whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted. When either
486	  parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting both
487	  counts every recorded fact;
488	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
489	  parameter is a `400 validation_error`;
490	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
491	  simply contains no facts, so every dimension reports its definite zero
492	  result.
493	
494	Each dimension is windowed by the occurrence time of its own fact: node
495	completions, failures, and retry consumption use the time of their recorded
496	node events; delivery outcomes use the delivery record's `occurred_at`
497	(shared by every attempt recorded in it); schedule triggers use the settled
498	period's trigger time; and the status distribution counts an execution at
499	the time it entered its current status — a still-running execution at its
500	start time, and a completed or terminated execution at the time of its
501	completion or termination event.
502	
503	### Export metrics in Prometheus text format
504	
505	```http
506	GET /metrics/export
507	X-Tenant-Id: acme
508	```
509	
510	A read-only tenant-scoped entry point that returns the same counts as the
511	metrics query — including the same optional `since` and `until` filters, the
512	same closed-interval semantics, the same definite zero result for a window
513	with `since` later than `until`, and the same `400 validation_error` for a
514	missing or empty tenant, a malformed timestamp, or an unknown query
515	parameter — rendered in the Prometheus text exposition format
516	(`text/plain; version=0.0.4`). It writes no events and no usage records.
517	
518	Each top-level metrics dimension is one metric family named with the
519	dimension's public key prefixed by `chronicleflow_`. The families appear in
520	the documented top-level key order, and the samples within a family are
521	ordered by ascending label value:
522	
523	- `chronicleflow_status_distribution` — samples carry a `status` label
524	  (`running`, `completed`, `terminated`); only the terminated samples also
525	  carry a `reason` label naming one of the four termination reasons;
526	- `chronicleflow_node_completions`, `chronicleflow_node_failures`, and
527	  `chronicleflow_retry_consumption` — samples carry a `node` label;
528	- `chronicleflow_schedule_triggers` — samples carry a `workflow` label;
529	- `chronicleflow_delivery_succeeded` and `chronicleflow_delivery_failed` —
530	  unlabeled scalar samples.
531	
532	Every value is a decimal integer. A dimension with no facts in the window
533	still exposes a zero-valued sample line (the labeled families expose one
534	unlabeled `0` sample). Every line ends with a newline and the whole document
535	ends with a single newline.
536	
537	The top-level keys appear in this order — status distribution, node
538	completions, node failures, retry consumption, delivery successes, delivery
539	failures, and schedule triggers:
540	
541	```json
542	{"status_distribution":{"running":1,"completed":2,"terminated":{"cancelled":0,"rejected":1,"retries_exhausted":0,"timeout":0}},"node_completions":{"charge":3},"node_failures":{"charge":2},"retry_consumption":{"charge":1},"delivery_succeeded":4,"delivery_failed":1,"schedule_triggers":{"nightly-orders":2}}
543	```
544	
545	- `status_distribution` — the tenant's executions divided into `running`,
546	  `completed`, and `terminated`; `terminated` is further broken down by
547	  termination reason, with every reason (`cancelled`, `rejected`,
548	  `retries_exhausted`, `timeout`) always present, zero when no execution
549	  ended for that reason.
550	- `node_completions` — persisted node completion facts per node identifier.
551	  Condition evaluations and skips are not completions and are never counted;
552	  a loop body node counts once per iteration it completes.
553	- `node_failures` — submitted task failures per node identifier; a loop body
554	  node accumulates each iteration's failures.
555	- `retry_consumption` — the number of times a failed task was re-queued for
556	  another attempt, per node identifier.
557	- `delivery_succeeded` and `delivery_failed` — outbound delivery attempts by
558	  outcome. Every attempt counts exactly once, so a delivery that fails and
559	  then succeeds on a later attempt records one of each.
560	- `schedule_triggers` — schedule periods that created an execution, per
561	  workflow identifier; settling the same period again counts nothing more.
562	
563	All counts are non-negative integers. A dimension with no facts reports zero
564	(or an empty group) rather than being omitted, and the groups within a
565	dimension are ordered by ascending identifier. Migrating an execution to
566	another version does not change attribution: facts recorded before and after
567	the migration accumulate under the same names. The optional `since` and
568	`until` filters and the Prometheus text export are described above.
569	
570	### Health
571	
572	```http
573	GET /health
574	```
575	
576	Returns `{"status":"ok"}`.

578	### Create a workflow
579	
580	```http
581	POST /workflows
582	Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1
583	
584	{
585	  "id": "order-flow",
586	  "nodes": [
587	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
588	    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
589	  ]
590	}
591	```
592	
593	Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
594	dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.
595	
596	A workflow definition may carry an optional `version` tag; declaring one
597	enables upgrades and keeps every version. Versioning is described under
598	"Workflow versions" below, and a workflow's stored versions and current
599	version are available through `GET /workflows/{id}`.
600	
601	A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:
602	
603	```json
604	{
605	  "id": "order-flow",
606	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
607	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
608	}
609	```
610	
611	See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
612	semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow (for a
613	versioned workflow, to executions bound to that version).
614	
615	A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:
616	
617	```json
618	{
619	  "id": "nightly-orders",
620	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
621	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
622	}
623	```
624	
625	See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.
626	
627	Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:
628	
629	```json
630	{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
631	```
632	
633	`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
634	is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
635	automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
636	compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
637	`false`.
638	
639	A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:
640	
641	```json
642	{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
643	```
644	
645	`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
646	task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
647	task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
648	dependencies of its successors.
649	
650	A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:
651	
652	```json
653	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
654	```
655	
656	`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
657	is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
658	attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
659	advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
660	permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
661	`retries_exhausted`.
662	
663	A task may instead declare an approval point:
664	
665	```json
666	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
667	```
668	
669	`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
670	identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
671	non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
672	approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
673	the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
674	consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
675	approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
676	execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
677	`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
678	writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
679	move the task.
680	
681	### Submit an approval decision
682	
683	```http
684	POST /executions/run-1/decision
685	Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1
686	
687	{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
688	```
689	
690	`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
691	exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
692	that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
693	decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
694	task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
695	execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
696	appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
697	rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
698	request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
699	`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
700	`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
701	Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
702	the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
703	returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
704	another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
705	approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
706	404.
707	
708	While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
709	cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
710	reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
711	pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
712	The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
713	reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
714	decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
715	waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
716	state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
717	approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
718	shape and event stream.
719	
720	A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
721	segment:
722	
723	```json
724	{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
725	```
726	
727	A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
728	and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
729	`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
730	integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the repeated segment anchored by
731	the entry task and the condition: it is the entry task, the condition, and
732	every node either anchor reaches through `depends_on`. The two anchors must
733	be connected — the condition gates the entry task (the entry depends on it)
734	or the condition is evaluated after the entry task (it depends on the entry),
735	as in the example above. The body keeps the usual DAG rules and always
736	contains the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
737	completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
738	overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
739	nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
740	loop node instead).
741	
742	When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
743	against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
744	nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
745	zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
746	iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
747	the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
748	are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
749	iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
750	evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
751	`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
752	`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
753	the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors. Once the loop
754	has finished, the execution-level `completed_nodes` list also includes every
755	body node that completed in any iteration, each listed only once and in the
756	order of its first completion, followed by the loop node itself; body nodes
757	skipped by a `run_if` guard remain out of the execution-level completed list
758	and are visible only in their iteration record. Body task outputs still
759	belong only to their iterations.
760	
761	Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
762	`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
763	`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
764	`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
765	records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
766	events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
767	exactly.
768	
769	### Dynamic map nodes
770	
771	A `map` node expands at runtime into one task instance per element of a
772	recorded array:
773	
774	```json
775	{"id": "ship", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["collect"],
776	 "source": "collect", "path": "items", "max_instances": 100,
777	 "template": {"id": "ship-item", "retries": 2}}
778	```
779	
780	A map node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `source`, `path`,
781	`max_instances`, and `template`; any other field is rejected as unknown.
782	
783	- `source` names a `task` node that is also listed in `depends_on`. Expansion
784	  begins only after every dependency has completed or been skipped; the
785	  element list comes solely from the source task's recorded output.
786	- `path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into that recorded output, using
787	  the same path syntax as a condition.
788	- `max_instances` is a positive integer bounding how many elements may
789	  expand.
790	- `template` describes the single task each instance runs and contains
791	  exactly an `id`, and optionally `retries` (an integer between 0 and 10,
792	  defaulting to 0) and an `approval` point with the same shape a task node
793	  uses. The template id only names the dynamically expanded instances; it
794	  may coincide with a declared node id or with another map's template id.
795	  A map node may also sit inside a loop body, expanding independently in
796	  every iteration (see "Maps inside loop bodies" below).
797	
798	When the dependencies settle, the value at `path` is read once. When it is an
799	array, one instance is created per element; the instances queue in ascending
800	element index order. Each `advance` still settles exactly one ready item, so
801	instances are worked in index order, one per call. An instance is an ordinary
802	task in every other respect: a submitted failure consumes the template's
803	retry bound and re-queues that instance, and a template approval point parks
804	the execution with the instance's `map_id` and `index` recorded, until an
805	approver decides it. Retries and approvals are per instance: results never
806	overwrite another instance.
807	
808	When every instance is completed, the map node completes and its output,
809	recorded both in the node's `outputs` entry and under its `maps` record, is
810	the list of instance outputs in ascending element order; its successors then
811	become available in the usual way.
812	
813	A value that is missing or is not an array expands to zero instances: the map
814	completes with an empty output list and releases its successors immediately.
815	When the array holds more elements than `max_instances`, no instance is
816	created at all: the map node fails permanently, is listed under
817	`failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`
818	under the usual exhaustion semantics.
819	
820	Execution state exposes each map under `maps`: the node's `status`
821	(`pending`, `running`, `completed`, or `failed`), one record per retained
822	instance giving its `index`, `status` (`ready`, `waiting`, `completed`, or
823	`failed`), its `output`, and its `failure_reason` (null except for a
824	permanently failed instance), plus the ordered completed `outputs` list and
825	the node's single `failure_reason`. A `ready` instance that has been
826	rewritten by a successful modify additionally carries that rewritten
827	`input`; every other instance record keeps exactly these fields. The `maps`
828	field is present only when the bound workflow declares a map node outside
829	any loop body; every other execution keeps its previous state shape.
830	
831	The event stream records a `map_expanded` event when expansion happens,
832	carrying the map id and the number of created instances (zero for a missing
833	or non-array value, and zero together with `exceeded` and the observed
834	element count when the bound is exceeded), and a `map_completed` event with
835	the map id and final instance count. Each instance's per-node events —
836	`node_completed`, `node_failed`, and `node_retried`, plus
837	`approval_requested` and `approval_decided` for a template approval point —
838	carry their `map_id` and element `index` alongside the template node id, so
839	replay rebuilds every instance solely from the event stream. Checkpoints are
840	written at instance boundaries, so recovery resumes with the unfinished
841	instances and never repeats an instance output. Per-instance completions and
842	failures count toward the existing node metrics under the template node id,
843	and webhook and queue subscriptions receive instance events exactly like any
844	other node event. Instance deletion and modification add their own
845	`instance_deleted` and `instance_modified` events, and re-expansion adds a
846	`map_reexpanded` event, described under
847	"Delete and modify expanded instances" below.
848	
849	### Maps inside loop bodies
850	
851	A map node may belong to a loop body — it is part of the body exactly when
852	the loop's entry or condition reaches it through `depends_on`, like any
853	other body member:
854	
855	```json
856	{"id": "fanout", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["attempt"],
857	 "source": "attempt", "path": "items", "max_instances": 10,
858	 "template": {"id": "work", "retries": 1}}
859	```
860	
861	A nested map expands once per iteration, when every dependency of its node
862	is completed or skipped in that iteration, and the element list is read from
863	the source task's output of that same iteration. The expansion rules are the
864	ones of an execution-level map: a missing path or a non-array value expands
865	to zero instances and the map completes for that iteration with an empty
866	output list, so the loop boundary is evaluated as usual; an element count
867	beyond `max_instances` creates no instance at all — the map fails
868	permanently, is listed under `failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates
869	with reason `retries_exhausted` under the usual exhaustion semantics.
870	
871	The expanded instances belong to their iteration only: they queue in
872	ascending element index order and are settled one per `advance`, exactly
873	like execution-level instances, and one iteration's instances never
874	overwrite another iteration's results. An instance is an ordinary task in
875	every other respect — a submitted failure consumes the template's retry
876	bound and re-queues that instance within its iteration, and a template
877	approval point parks the execution until an approver decides it — with no
878	influence from the iteration number.
879	
880	Iteration state exposes each nested map under the iteration record's `maps`
881	field, with the same per-map shape as an execution-level map (`status`, one
882	record per instance, the ordered completed `outputs`, and `failure_reason`);
883	the field is present on every iteration of a loop whose body declares a map
884	node. When a nested map completes, its node enters the iteration's
885	`completed_nodes` and its output list is recorded in the iteration's
886	`outputs`; when the loop finishes, the usual roll-up lists the map node once
887	in the execution-level `completed_nodes`, while its outputs stay with their
888	iterations. An execution-level `maps` field is not created for nested maps.
889	
890	Every event a nested expansion records carries the owning `loop_id` and
891	`iteration` alongside the map id and, for per-instance events, the element
892	`index`: `map_expanded`, `map_completed`, the per-instance `node_completed`,
893	`node_failed`, and `node_retried`, and `approval_requested` and
894	`approval_decided` for a template approval point. The `iteration_started`
895	event of a loop whose body declares map nodes carries the iteration's
896	initial `maps` skeleton, so replay rebuilds every iteration's instance list,
897	status, and ownership solely from the event stream, consistent with the
898	materialized state. Checkpoints are written at each iteration's instance
899	boundaries, so recovery continues the current iteration's unfinished
900	instances and never repeats an instance output. Cancellation, timeouts,
901	leases, retries, and approvals keep their existing semantics, and a nested
902	map never changes an execution's termination reason.
903	
904	Executions whose workflows declare no nested map behave exactly as before:
905	state fields, event contents, and advancement results are unchanged.
906	
907	### Delete and modify expanded instances
908	
909	An expanded dynamic node offers, alongside expansion and per-instance
910	advancement, two instance-level operations and a node-level re-expansion.
911	All three are ordinary idempotent HTTP commands over the same entry points
912	the rest of the service uses; they introduce no second protocol.
913	
914	An instance that has never advanced can be removed, and so can an instance
915	that has permanently failed:
916	
917	```http
918	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/2/delete
919	Idempotency-Key: delete-instance-2
920	
921	{}
922	```
923	
924	The body must be an empty object. Removing an instance drops only that
925	instance's record: every retained instance keeps its element index, its
926	place in the queue, and its advancement order. When the removed instance was
927	the map's last unfinished instance, the node completes under the existing
928	rules with an output list containing only the retained instances' outputs,
929	in ascending element-index order, and its successors unlock as usual. An
930	instance that is waiting on an approval, or has already completed, can never
931	be deleted; attempting it returns `409 conflict` and changes no state. A
932	permanently failed instance is removable after the execution has terminated,
933	but removing it never revives the execution, alters its termination reason,
934	or changes the node's failed conclusion. When every retained instance of a
935	map inside a loop body has ended, the iteration's other nodes advance as
936	usual and the node completes or ends under the existing rules; deleting an
937	instance in one iteration never touches another iteration.
938	
939	An instance that has never advanced can also have its input rewritten
940	before it is worked:
941	
942	```http
943	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/1/modify
944	Idempotency-Key: modify-instance-1
945	
946	{"input":{"address":"742 Evergreen Terrace"}}
947	```
948	
949	The body must contain exactly `input`, an object with the new content; it is
950	validated like every other request body (finite numbers only). The rewrite
951	changes only the parameters used when that one instance is later advanced:
952	it affects no other instance, and the output and history of an instance that
953	has already advanced (waiting, completed, or permanently failed) are
954	immutable — modifying such an instance returns `409 conflict` and changes no
955	state. The rewritten input, including its full float precision and `-0.0`,
956	is stored verbatim.
957	
958	Delete and modify calls on the same instance settle in call order: every
959	call applies to the instance list exactly as the earlier calls left it, and
960	several calls on one instance each take effect independently, one after
961	another. A rewritten instance has still never advanced, so it remains
962	deletable; deleting or modifying an instance an earlier call already
963	removed is a `404 not_found`; and a second rewrite of the same instance
964	records the first rewrite's content as its `before`.
965	
966	Both commands apply to a map nested in a loop body exactly as to an
967	execution-level map: the current running iteration's instances are
968	addressed by the same path, and every event they append carries the owning
969	`loop_id` and `iteration` alongside the map id; an execution-level instance
970	carries no loop context.
971	
972	An out-of-bounds element index, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic
973	`map`, a missing execution, or a cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found`
974	and writes nothing. A missing or mistyped field, a non-object modify
975	`input`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a `400 validation_error`
976	with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a
977	`409 conflict`; repeating the same command with the same key returns the
978	first result and appends no second event.
979	
980	Every successful call appends exactly one event to the execution stream:
981	
982	- an `instance_deleted` event records the action type, the owning dynamic
983	  node under `map_id`, the removed instance's element `index` and `status`
984	  (`ready` or `failed`), and, for a map inside a loop body, the `loop_id`
985	  and `iteration`;
986	- an `instance_modified` event records the action type, the owning
987	  `map_id`, the instance `index`, the content `before` the rewrite (`null`
988	  for an instance that had never been rewritten) and `after` it, and the
989	  same loop context when the instance belongs to an iteration.
990	
991	Replay rebuilds the instance list, every instance's status and ownership,
992	and each rewrite solely from the event stream: a delete drops the recorded
993	instance (and the subsequent `map_completed`, when the deletion finished the
994	node, completes it with the retained outputs), and a modify applies the
995	rewritten input to that one instance, so the rebuilt state is exactly the
996	materialized state. A checkpoint is written at the instance boundary of
997	every successful delete or modify; after a restart recovery continues the
998	unfinished instances, repeats no instance output, and never resurrects a
999	deleted instance. The operations change no advancement conclusion or
1000	termination semantics: cancellation, timeouts, approvals, leases, retries,
1001	and retry exhaustion keep their existing behavior. Executions that never
1002	use deletion, modification, or re-expansion keep exactly their current
1003	state fields, event contents, and advancement results.
1004	
1005	### Re-expand a dynamic node
1006	
1007	A dynamic node that has already expanded can be expanded again on demand —
1008	above all to regenerate its instance list after deletions:
1009	
1010	```http
1011	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/reexpand
1012	Idempotency-Key: reexpand-1
1013	
1014	{}
1015	```
1016	
1017	(The same operation is also accepted at `.../maps/ship/expand`.) The body
1018	must be an empty object. Re-expansion reads the element list again from the
1019	source task's recorded output — the same recorded output the first
1020	expansion read, which never changes once recorded — and regenerates the
1021	instance list from it: every previous instance record is replaced, and the
1022	fresh instances queue from element index zero in ascending order. The
1023	regenerated instances are ordinary instances in every respect: they are
1024	deleted, modified, advanced, retried, and approved through the same entries
1025	and with exactly the same behavior as a first expansion, and their retry
1026	bounds start from zero.
1027	
1028	Every successful call appends exactly one `map_reexpanded` event, recording
1029	the action type, the owning dynamic node under `map_id`, and the number of
1030	generated instances under `instance_count`; for a map inside a loop body
1031	the event also carries the owning `loop_id` and `iteration`, and only the
1032	current running iteration's expansion is replaced. A node that had
1033	completed returns to `running`: it leaves `completed_nodes`, its recorded
1034	output entry is discarded, and when the regenerated instances have all
1035	completed the node completes again under the existing rules, its result
1036	list holding only the finally retained instances' outputs in ascending
1037	element-index order. An empty element list completes the node again at
1038	once with an empty output list, exactly like a zero-element first
1039	expansion.
1040	
1041	Re-expansion is rejected with `409 conflict` and writes nothing when the
1042	node has not expanded yet, when it has permanently failed, when one of its
1043	instances is waiting on an approval decision, when the execution has
1044	already completed, or when a nested map's loop is not currently running.
1045	A terminated execution's unfinished node may still be re-expanded; doing so
1046	never revives the execution or alters its termination reason. A missing
1047	execution, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic `map`, or a
1048	cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found` and writes nothing. A
1049	non-empty or non-object body, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
1050	`400 validation_error` with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key
1051	from another operation is a `409 conflict`; repeating the same call with
1052	the same key returns the first result and appends no second event. Replay
1053	rebuilds the regenerated instance list, statuses, and ownership solely
1054	from the event stream, a checkpoint is written at the re-expansion
1055	boundary, and recovery after a restart continues the unfinished
1056	regenerated instances — repeating no instance output and never resurrecting
1057	an instance that stayed deleted.
1058	
1059	### Workflow versions
1060	
1061	A workflow can declare a version tag alongside its nodes:
1062	
1063	```json
1064	{
1065	  "id": "order-flow",
1066	  "version": "2026-09-25",
1067	  "nodes": [
1068	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
1069	    {"id": "ship", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
1070	  ]
1071	}
1072	```
1073	
1074	`version` is an optional non-empty string of at most 100 characters, validated
1075	like every other identifier. Posting it when the workflow does not yet exist
1076	creates the workflow with that version; posting another definition with a new
1077	`version` to the same `id` adds a new version without touching the previous
1078	ones — the workflow keeps its entire history, and every stored version remains
1079	usable. The most recently added version becomes the workflow's current
1080	version. Posting a definition without a `version` to an existing workflow
1081	still conflicts, and reusing a version tag already stored for the same
1082	workflow is a `409 conflict`; either rejection writes nothing.
1083	
1084	A version declaration may also carry `subscriptions` and a `schedule`,
1085	validated exactly like at creation. Subscriptions are attached to the
1086	declared version and apply only to executions bound to it; a version without
1087	subscriptions replaces none, and other versions' subscriptions stay intact.
1088	Declaring a `schedule` on an added version replaces the workflow's single
1089	schedule plan in the usual way (re-anchored, pause flag kept).
1090	
1091	An execution created without an explicit `version` binds to the workflow's
1092	current version at the moment it starts:
1093	
1094	```http
1095	POST /executions
1096	Idempotency-Key: execution-versioned
1097	
1098	{"id":"run-v2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{}}
1099	```
1100	
1101	An execution may instead name the version it wants:
1102	
1103	```json
1104	{"id":"run-v1","workflow_id":"order-flow","version":"2026-08-01","input":{}}
1105	```
1106	
1107	Naming a version that does not exist for the workflow is a missing-resource
1108	`404 not_found`, exactly like naming a workflow that does not exist; the
1109	execution is not created. Everything about an execution follows its bound
1110	version: ready-node selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval
1111	points, retry counts, leases, and the subscriptions that fire for its events.
1112	Adding a new version never interrupts an execution already running: an
1113	execution started before the upgrade keeps advancing on its old version to
1114	completion or termination. Its checkpoints are snapshots of the same state,
1115	recovery rebuilds from the bound version, and replay rebuilds state and the
1116	version binding solely from its event stream; recorded events and historical
1117	conclusions never change.
1118	
1119	A versioned execution's state carries its `version` tag, and its
1120	`execution_started` event records the same tag; querying it therefore shows
1121	which version it is bound to. A workflow that never declares a version, and an
1122	execution of one, keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
1123	stream with no added field.
1124	
1125	The definition query lists every version and the current one:
1126	
1127	```http
1128	GET /workflows/order-flow
1129	```
1130	
1131	```json
1132	{"current_version":"2026-09-25","id":"order-flow","versions":[
1133	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-08-01"},
1134	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-09-25"}
1135	]}
1136	```
1137	
1138	Versions are returned in declaration order; each entry is the stored
1139	definition with its `version` tag. A workflow that never declared a version
1140	returns a single untagged entry and `current_version: null`. A missing
1141	workflow returns 404 `not_found`. Cross-tenant references are missing
1142	resources as usual.
1143	
1144	### Migrate a running execution to another version
1145	
1146	```http
1147	POST /executions/run-v1/migrate
1148	Idempotency-Key: migrate-request-1
1149	
1150	{"version":"2026-09-25"}
1151	```
1152	
1153	A running execution can be explicitly moved to another declared version of
1154	the same workflow; after the call it keeps advancing under the new version.
1155	The body must contain exactly `version`, a non-empty version identifier that
1156	names a stored version of the execution's workflow. On success a
1157	`version_migrated` event is appended to the event stream — it records the
1158	`from_version`, the `to_version`, and the structural skeleton of the target
1159	revision (its `loops`, and, when it declares approval points, its
1160	`waiting_approval` and `approvals` fields) — and a checkpoint of the rebound
1161	state is written at that same node boundary. The execution's state then
1162	carries the target version.
1163	
1164	Everything that follows uses the target version's definition: ready-node
1165	selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval points, retries, and
1166	the workflow subscriptions that fire for later events. Everything recorded
1167	before the migration is kept exactly as-is: prior events, node outputs,
1168	condition conclusions, and per-iteration history are never rewritten. Loops
1169	introduced by the target definition begin in their initial pending state; a
1170	loop the old definition knew keeps its recorded iterations and conclusion.
1171	Replay rebuilds the migration point and version binding solely from the
1172	event stream, and after a restart recovery continues on the migrated version
1173	from the migration checkpoint, so checkpoints and materialized state agree.
1174	
1175	An execution parked at an approval point may also be migrated: the waiting
1176	point keeps its recorded node and approver list unchanged (only a recorded
1177	approver may still decide it), and once the decision lands the subsequent
1178	advancement follows the target version. Executions that are never migrated
1179	keep advancing on the version they started with to completion or
1180	termination; adding versions never moves them. An execution of a workflow
1181	that never declared a version cannot name a target, and such workflows and
1182	their executions keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
1183	content.
1184	
1185	The response is the updated execution state. Migrating a `completed` or
1186	`terminated` execution returns `409 conflict` and changes nothing. A missing
1187	execution or a target version that does not exist for the workflow returns
1188	`404 not_found`; a cross-tenant reference is the same missing resource. A
1189	missing or mistyped `version`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
1190	`400 validation_error`. Migrating a running execution to the version it is
1191	already bound to returns the current state as-is, appending no event and
1192	writing no checkpoint; a `completed` or `terminated` execution instead
1193	returns `409 conflict` even when the target version is exactly the one it is
1194	bound to. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a `409
1195	conflict`. The migration event is listed directly by the per-execution
1196	events query, and node outputs produced after the migration belong to the
1197	target version's definition. Approver-list validation, lease renewal, and
1198	delivery history keep their existing semantics before and after a migration.
1199	
1200	### Start an execution
1201	
1202	```http
1203	POST /executions
1204	Idempotency-Key: execution-request-1
1205	
1206	{"id":"run-1","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{"order_id":"o-7"}}
1207	```
1208	
1209	Returns HTTP 201. The execution starts in `running` state. Without an
1210	explicit `version`, it binds to the workflow's current version at start time;
1211	naming a `version` binds to that one instead (and a missing version is a
1212	`404 not_found`). See "Workflow versions" for the binding and upgrade rules.
1213	
1214	An execution may declare a timeout:
1215	
1216	```json
1217	{"id":"run-2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{},"timeout_seconds":30}
1218	```
1219	
1220	`timeout_seconds` is a positive number of seconds counted from the moment the
1221	execution starts. Once the deadline passes, the execution terminates with
1222	termination reason `timeout` and no longer accepts output. Executions without
1223	a timeout never expire.
1224	
1225	An execution may also declare its own webhook `subscriptions`, which apply in
1226	addition to the ones its workflow declares:
1227	
1228	```json
1229	{
1230	  "id": "run-3",
1231	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
1232	  "input": {},
1233	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/ops", "events": ["node_completed"], "max_attempts": 3}]
1234	}
1235	```
1236	
1237	### List workflows
1238	
1239	```http
1240	GET /workflows?limit=50
1241	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1242	```
1243	
1244	Enumerates the workflows declared in the request's namespace. The response
1245	is `{"workflows":[{"id":"order-flow"}, ...]}`: one entry per workflow, each
1246	carrying its identifier, in ascending identifier order. A namespace with no
1247	workflows gets the definite empty result `{"workflows":[]}`, not an error.
1248	The query is read-only: it creates nothing, appends no events, and records
1249	no usage, so repeating it returns the same answer and changes no stored
1250	state.
1251	
1252	The list is paged with a keyset cursor:
1253	
1254	- `limit` — required; the maximum number of entries in the page, a positive
1255	  integer. The page never holds more entries than the limit;
1256	- `cursor` — optional; the identifier of the previous page's last entry.
1257	  Only entries whose identifier sorts strictly after the cursor are
1258	  returned, so paging with the previous page's last identifier yields
1259	  consecutive pages that neither overlap nor skip. A cursor past the end
1260	  returns the definite empty list.
1261	
1262	### List executions
1263	
1264	```http
1265	GET /executions?workflow_id=order-flow&status=terminated&termination_reason=timeout&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=run-41&limit=50
1266	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1267	```
1268	
1269	Enumerates the executions in the request's namespace in ascending execution
1270	identifier order. The response is `{"executions":[...]}`; each entry carries
1271	the execution `id`, its `workflow_id`, its `status` (`running`, `completed`,
1272	or `terminated`, always a string), its `termination_reason` (one of the
1273	four termination reasons for a terminated execution, otherwise `null`), and
1274	its `created_at` (the ISO-8601 UTC creation timestamp ending in `Z`), in
1275	that stable key order. A namespace with no executions gets the definite
1276	empty result `{"executions":[]}`. Like the workflows list this query is
1277	read-only and never settles a due timeout, appends an event, writes a
1278	checkpoint, or records usage, so repeated calls return the same answer and
1279	change no state or metering conclusion.
1280	
1281	The same `limit` and `cursor` pagination applies, with the cursor taken
1282	from the previous page's last execution identifier. In addition, five
1283	filters may be combined, and every given filter must match:
1284	
1285	- `workflow_id` — only executions of that workflow. Referencing a workflow
1286	  the namespace does not contain, including one owned by another tenant, is
1287	  the usual `404 not_found` and reveals nothing about its existence;
1288	- `status` — only executions in that lifecycle status. A value other than
1289	  `running`, `completed`, or `terminated` is a `400 validation_error`;
1290	- `termination_reason` — only executions that terminated for exactly that
1291	  reason. The filter is meaningful solely for terminated executions:
1292	  running and completed executions never appear under it, even when other
1293	  filters are given alongside it. An unknown reason is a
1294	  `400 validation_error`;
1295	- `since` and `until` — the same closed creation-time bounds the events and
1296	  metrics queries accept: each is an ISO-8601 UTC timestamp ending in `Z`,
1297	  and an execution whose `created_at` equals `since` or `until` is
1298	  returned. When either parameter is absent the corresponding bound is
1299	  open, so omitting both returns exactly the unfiltered list; a malformed
1300	  timestamp is a `400 validation_error`. When `since` is later than
1301	  `until` the window matches nothing and the result is the definite empty
1302	  list, not an error.
1303	
1304	Both list endpoints follow the usual tenant scope: omitting
1305	`X-Tenant-Id` keeps the single legacy namespace, and a tenant sees only its
1306	own workflows and executions under every combination of filters. Every
1307	parameter may appear at most once; a repeated parameter, an unknown
1308	parameter, a missing `limit`, or a `limit` that is not a positive integer is
1309	a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing.
1310	
1311	### Inspect an execution
1312	
1313	```http
1314	GET /executions/run-1
1315	GET /executions/run-1/events
1316	GET /executions/run-1/checkpoints
1317	```
1318	
1319	The first endpoint returns the materialized state. The second returns the
1320	ordered event stream. The third returns the ordered checkpoints; each entry
1321	gives its `sequence`, the `event_sequence` position it was taken at, the full
1322	`state` summary, and `created_at`.
1323	
1324	The events query is read-only: it appends no events, records no usage, and
1325	changes no state, so advancement, approvals, recovery, and replay never alter
1326	what it observes. With no query parameters it returns the complete ordered
1327	event list exactly as before. It also accepts optional filter and pagination
1328	parameters, which combine as an intersection:
1329	
1330	```http
1331	GET /executions/run-1/events?types=node_completed,node_failed&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
1332	```
1333	
1334	- `types` — a comma-separated set of event types; only events whose type is
1335	  in the set are returned. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown
1336	  event type is a `400 validation_error`;
1337	- `since` and `until` — the same closed-interval occurrence-time bounds the
1338	  metrics query accepts: an event whose time equals either boundary is
1339	  returned. When `since` is later than `until` the window matches nothing and
1340	  the result is an empty list, not an error;
1341	- `cursor` — the sequence of the last event of the previous page; only events
1342	  with a strictly greater sequence are returned;
1343	- `limit` — the maximum number of events in the page, in ascending sequence
1344	  order.
1345	
1346	Every parameter may appear at most once; a repeated parameter, an unknown
1347	parameter, a malformed timestamp, or a cursor or limit that is not a positive
1348	integer is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Filtering never
1349	renumbers events, so paging with `cursor` set to the previous page's last
1350	sequence yields consecutive pages that neither overlap nor skip. A filter
1351	that matches nothing returns the definite empty result `{"events":[]}`, and
1352	querying a missing or another tenant's execution is the usual
1353	`404 not_found`.
1354	
1355	### Webhook notifications
1356	
1357	Subscriptions declared on a workflow or an execution deliver outbound webhook
1358	messages when business events occur. Each webhook subscription contains exactly:
1359	
1360	- `url`: a non-empty `http` or `https` address to POST to;
1361	- `events`: a non-empty array of event types without duplicates, drawn from
1362	  `node_completed`, `execution_completed`, `execution_terminated`, and
1363	  `approval_decided` (a termination is the same event type whatever its
1364	  reason);
1365	- `timeout_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds to wait for each
1366	  delivery attempt, defaulting to 5;
1367	- `max_attempts` (optional): an integer between 1 and 10, defaulting to 1.
1368	
1369	Any other field, a missing `url` or `events`, a mistyped value, an empty or
1370	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
1371	a non-finite number, a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than
1372	ten attempts is a 400 `validation_error` and rejects the whole request — no
1373	workflow, execution, or subscription is partially written. A subscription
1374	may instead declare a queue target (`queue` instead of `url`); see "Queue
1375	subscriptions" below.
1376	
1377	When a subscribed event occurs, a JSON message is POSTed to each matching
1378	target immediately: the body carries `event_type`, `execution_id`, and the
1379	event's details (such as `node_id` for a completed node or `approver` for an
1380	approval decision). Each delivery request carries an `Idempotency-Key`
1381	header; retries of the same event reuse the same key, and different events
1382	never share a key. A delivery is attempted at most the subscription's
1383	`max_attempts` times, with an increasing backoff between attempts. An
1384	unreachable target, a timeout, or a non-2xx response marks the attempt as
1385	failed, but a failed delivery never changes the outcome of the call that
1386	triggered it.
1387	
1388	Deliveries do not append execution events, do not add fields to the execution
1389	state, and are never triggered by replay, recovery, or queries, so
1390	checkpoints and replay conclusions are unaffected. An execution that declares
1391	no subscriptions keeps exactly the same state, event stream, and advancement
1392	results as before.
1393	
1394	### Inspect the delivery history
1395	
1396	```http
1397	GET /executions/run-1/deliveries
1398	```
1399	
1400	Returns `{"deliveries": [...]}` in the order the events occurred. Each record
1401	gives its `sequence`, the subscription `url`, the `event_type`, the
1402	`event_sequence` that triggered it, the delivery `idempotency_key`, the final
1403	`status` (`delivered` or `failed`), the `attempt_count`, an `attempts` list
1404	recording each try's `status_code` or `error` (so a retry that eventually
1405	succeeds is visible attempt by attempt), and `occurred_at`. Querying the
1406	history of a missing execution returns 404 `not_found` and records nothing.
1407	Every delivery attempt is recorded, including one whose history record itself
1408	could not be written: such a failure is not swallowed — it is retried once in
1409	a fresh write carrying `status` `failed` and a `persistence_error` describing
1410	the write failure, so the attempt remains visible whenever the database can
1411	accept it (and is logged rather than silently dropped if it cannot).
1412	
1413	### Queue subscriptions
1414	
1415	A subscription may declare a queue target instead of a webhook `url`:
1416	
1417	```json
1418	{
1419	  "id": "run-4",
1420	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
1421	  "input": {},
1422	  "subscriptions": [{"queue": "order-events", "events": ["node_completed"], "visibility_seconds": 60}]
1423	}
1424	```
1425	
1426	A queue subscription contains exactly:
1427	
1428	- `queue`: a non-empty queue name of any length;
1429	- `events`: the same non-empty event-type list a webhook subscription takes;
